t: Sum of Matrix After Queries — Reverse Processing
o: We apply row/column 'paint' queries to an n×n grid and need the final total. Building the matrix is impossible (n up to 10^4 ⇒ 10^8 cells). Key observation: a cell's final value is determined by the LAST query touching its row or column. So instead of simulating forward, walk the queries backward: the first time (in reverse) we see a row, that query fixes every cell of that row that isn't later fixed by a column query, contributing val × (number of columns not yet claimed by column queries). Example 1 reversed: [1,0,4] fixes column 0 (3 cells), [0,2,3] fixes row 2 minus col 0 (2 cells), [1,2,2] fixes column 2 minus rows 0,2 (1 cell), [0,0,1] fixes row 0 minus cols 0,2 (1 cell) → 12+6+2+1... matching totals of 23 with the actual values.
k: Process queries in reverse; the earliest-in-reverse query touching a line owns its unclaimed cells.

a.i: Maintain sets of already-finalized rows and columns. Scanning queries backwards, a row query adds val×(n − |finalized columns|) cells if that row wasn't finalized yet, then marks it. Symmetric for columns. Every cell is counted exactly once by its last writer.
s: Initialize empty sets seenRows, seenCols and answer 0.
Iterate queries from last to first.
Row query with unseen index: add val*(n - seenCols.size()), mark row seen.
Column query symmetric; return the accumulated sum.
a.t: O(q) — each query processed once with O(1) set work
a.sp: O(n) for the two seen sets

w: The reverse-sweep trick is the whole problem; forward simulation or building the matrix will TLE. Pitfall: use 64-bit sums (up to ~5·10^4 × 10^4 × 10^5). Follow-up: what if queries were point updates instead of full rows/columns?
